title: Rusticus lends a book
hookLine: from Rusticus: that his character needed correcting, and a copy of Epictetus (Meditations 1.7)
last: FACTIO — WATCH THE RACE, KEEP YOUR HEAD.

lines: YOU'LL LOVE IT. YOU NEED IT.
cards: A book handed over with two words: read this. Maybe it got read. Maybe it's still on a shelf with the giver's name inside.
It's a strange kind of gift, because it says two things at once: I think you'll love this, and, I think you need it. The seventh entry in book one is about a man who told the future emperor both.
He said his character needed work, and he lent him a book by a former slave.

teach.b: First, the correction. In Long's translation the entry opens: "From Rusticus I received the impression that my character required improvement and discipline."
A young man who would rule the Roman world, writing years later, with gratitude, that someone had told him he needed fixing. Second, what Rusticus steered him away from.
Not to get carried away with clever speeches and showy writing. Not to parade around as a philosopher, doing exercises to be admired.

teach.h: NO SHOW; READ CAREFULLY; WRITE PLAIN.
teach.b: To read carefully, not skim, and not agree too quickly with people who just talk well. To write letters plainly, like the one Rusticus wrote to Marcus's mother from Sinuessa, a town on the coast.
And to be easy to reconcile with people who'd offended him, as soon as they were willing. Third, the book.
Last of all, Marcus thanks Rusticus for introducing him to the discourses of Epictetus, from his own copy. Follow the chain. Epictetus, born a slave, teaches in Nicopolis.
Students take notes; Arrian's are the ones that survive, though no one can be sure his are the ones Rusticus had. A copy reaches Rome. Rusticus hands it to the emperor's heir.
And the emperor's notebook, full of Epictetus, reaches you.
Fourth, what a lent book carries: the friend's trust, and sometimes their correction.
Rusticus didn't lecture Marcus about his character forever. He said it once, and then gave him something better to read.

how: Some readers of the Stoics pass their copies on, and give the Meditations as a gift between friends, mentors and students.

o: the slave who copied out Epictetus's lectures by hand
the teacher who corrected Marcus and lent him Epictetus
the farmer who ran Marcus's country estate outside Rome

games.q: Rusticus lends a book — tap the pairs.
p: where Rusticus wrote a plain letter

s: Marcus resented Rusticus for criticizing his character
he lists it first among his thanks.
Rusticus lent Marcus a copy of Epictetus' discourses from his own collection
the emperor learned from a former slave's teaching through a friend's book.
Rusticus encouraged Marcus to give showy philosophical speeches
he steered him away from showy writing and display.

games.q: you're Rusticus. a gifted young man, heir to the empire, is drawn to clever speeches and showy writing. what do you do?
o: tell him his character needs work, then lend him Epictetus.
say nothing; it's not your place.
games.why: Rusticus corrected him and handed him a book. Marcus thanks him for both, by name.

practice: Think of a book that changed something in you, and picture the person who handed it over or told you about it; thank them silently.
Then think of someone who might need that book, or another one, right now: not to fix them, but to give them something better than advice.

wordCard.voice: Rusticus. The teacher who told young Marcus his character needed work, and then gave him his own copy of Epictetus. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: notes, memoranda. Marcus's word for the discourses of Epictetus Rusticus shared.

carryVoice: Your line: pass the book on. A lent book carries trust. That's day five hundred twenty-four.
